question: A previously healthy 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of upper back pain, dyspnea, and a sensation of pressure in his chest. He has had no shortness of breath, palpitations, fevers, or chills. He emigrated from Ecuador when he was 5 years old. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. He takes no medications. He is 194 cm (6 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 70.3 kg (155 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m2. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 73/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 152/86 mm Hg in the right arm and 130/72 mg Hg in the left arm. Pulmonary examination shows faint inspiratory wheezing bilaterally. A CT scan of the chest with contrast is shown. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

enhanced_information: The patient presents with upper back pain, dyspnea, and a sensation of pressure in the chest, alongside notable blood pressure discrepancies between arms. The CT scan likely reveals an aortic abnormality. Given the age and symptoms, congenital narrowing of the aortic arch is a plausible cause, as it can lead to upper back pain and dyspnea due to compromised blood flow. Cystic medial necrosis is also a consideration, particularly if the CT shows aortic dilation, as it can lead to dissection, which aligns with the symptoms. However, the patient's young age and low BMI make atherosclerotic plaque formation less likely. Chagas disease, while relevant due to the patient's background, is less likely to present with isolated back pain and dyspnea without other systemic symptoms. Large-vessel vasculitis is also less common in this demographic without systemic signs. Therefore, the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition is congenital narrowing of the aortic arch, supported by the CT findings and symptomatology.
analysis: The patient presents with upper back pain, dyspnea, and a sensation of pressure in the chest, along with a significant difference in blood pressure readings between the arms. These symptoms, combined with the patient's young age and background, suggest a vascular issue. The discrepancy in blood pressure indicates possible obstruction or narrowing of the aorta, which is consistent with congenital conditions. Congenital narrowing of the aortic arch (coarctation) is known to cause upper body symptoms due to reduced blood flow and can lead to hypertension in the upper body and hypotension in the lower body. While cystic medial necrosis could lead to aortic dissection, it is less likely in a young, previously healthy individual without other risk factors. Atherosclerotic plaque formation is also unlikely given the patient's age and low BMI. Infection with Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease) is less likely to present in this manner without systemic symptoms. Large-vessel vasculitis is also less common in this demographic without systemic signs. Therefore, the most likely underlying cause of this patient's condition is congenital narrowing of the aortic arch, supported by the clinical presentation and expected CT findings.
